title: What basic safety training does STCW require for seafarers, and how often is the refresher?
description: STCW basic training under Code section A-VI/1, the five yearly proof of competence, and how AMSA and the US Coast Guard apply it, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The International Maritime Organization's STCW Convention requires seafarers to complete basic training in four areas set out in section A-VI/1 of the STCW Code: personal survival techniques, fire prevention and firefighting, elementary first aid, and personal safety and social responsibilities. Since the 2010 Manila amendments, seafarers must show every five years that they have maintained that competence. Flag states apply this nationally: the Australian Maritime Safety Authority through Marine Orders and the United States Coast Guard through 46 CFR.
keyTakeaways: The STCW Convention was adopted on July 7, 1978 and entered into force on April 28, 1984; Part A of the STCW Code is mandatory and Part B is guidance.

Basic training covers four competence tables in the STCW Code: A-VI/1-1 personal survival techniques, A-VI/1-2 fire prevention and firefighting, A-VI/1-3 elementary first aid and A-VI/1-4 personal safety and social responsibilities.

In the United States, 46 CFR 11.302 and 12.602 require evidence every 5 years of maintaining basic training competence, with some elements provable through one year of sea service in the last five and others only through approved shore assessment.

In Australia, a certificate of safety training requires a course complying with STCW Code section A-VI/1 paragraph 2 plus security awareness, and revalidation under Marine Order 73 requires either 12 months of sea service in five years or approved refresher courses.
IMO is conducting a comprehensive review of STCW; as at November 2026 the target completion date is 2029 to 2030 and current requirements continue to apply.
jurisdiction: International (IMO), with Australian (Commonwealth) and United States (federal) implementation
regulator: International Maritime Organization (IMO); Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA); United States Coast Guard (USCG)
appliesTo: Seafarers employed or engaged on seagoing ships with designated safety or pollution prevention duties
Ship owners, operators and crewing agencies that must ensure crew hold valid STCW certificates
Maritime training providers delivering approved basic training and refresher courses
Officers and ratings revalidating STCW endorsements or certificates every five years

sections.heading: What is the STCW Convention and how is it structured?

blocks.text: The International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers, 1978 (STCW) is the IMO treaty that sets minimum training and certification standards for seafarers on seagoing ships. According to [IMO](https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/HumanElement/Pages/STCW-Conv-LINK.aspx), it was adopted on July 7, 1978 and entered into force on April 28, 1984.

The 1995 amendments, in force from February 1, 1997, introduced the STCW Code. IMO describes the split simply: "Part A of the Code is mandatory. Part B is recommended." The 2010 Manila amendments, adopted on June 25, 2010 and in force from January 1, 2012, added requirements including security training, leadership and teamwork, ECDIS training and revised hours of work and rest.

STCW is implemented by each flag state. That is why a training manager must read both the Convention text and the national rules of the flag under which crew are certified. This page uses Australia and the United States as worked examples.

sections.heading: What does STCW basic training cover?

blocks.text: Basic training covers four competence areas, each defined by a table in section A-VI/1 of the STCW Code. The US implementing rule, [46 CFR 11.302](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-46/section-11.302), lists them against the Code tables it incorporates by reference.

items: **Personal survival techniques** (Table A-VI/1-1), such as donning lifejackets and immersion suits, boarding survival craft and righting an inverted liferaft.
**Fire prevention and firefighting** (Table A-VI/1-2), including use of extinguishers and breathing apparatus and fighting fires in smoke filled spaces.

blocks.text: STCW Code tables are written as competences with methods for demonstrating them and criteria for evaluating them. In practice this makes basic training an early example of [competency-based training](/glossary/competency-based-training): completion alone is not the standard, demonstrated competence is.

sections.heading: How often must seafarers refresh basic training?

blocks.text: Every five years. Since the Manila amendments, seafarers qualified in basic training must provide evidence every five years of maintaining the required standard of competence. The rule text is in the STCW Code, and each flag state sets out how that evidence is accepted.

The US text is explicit. [46 CFR 11.302(b)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-46/section-11.302) states that "every 5 years seafarers qualified in accordance with § 11.301(c) and (d) of this subpart must provide evidence of maintaining the standard of competence for BT", and [46 CFR 12.602(b)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-46/section-12.602) applies the same five year rule to rating endorsements. The Coast Guard then divides the evidence into two kinds:

items: **Accepted through sea service:** one year of sea service within the last five years counts for listed elements such as donning a lifejacket, boarding survival craft, using breathing apparatus, a smoke filled space rescue, elementary first aid and personal safety and social responsibilities.

**Shore assessment only:** the Coast Guard "will only accept evidence of approved assessments conducted ashore" for elements such as donning and using an immersion suit, jumping from a height into water, righting an inverted liferaft, swimming in a lifejacket, keeping afloat without one, and live fire extinguishing exercises.
**No recent sea service:** applicants without one year of sea service in the last five years must meet the full standard again or complete approved or accepted refresher training.

blocks.title: Sea service does not replace live drills
blocks.text: Under the US rule, even a seafarer with continuous sea service needs an approved shore assessment every five years for the practical survival and live firefighting elements, because those cannot safely be repeated aboard.

sections.heading: How does Australia apply STCW basic training through AMSA?

blocks.text: AMSA issues a certificate of safety training under the Navigation Act 2012, with eligibility and revalidation set in Marine Orders. Under section 22 of [Marine Order 70 (Seafarer certification) 2014](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2014L00177/latest), the applicant must be at least 16 years old and have completed an approved course that complies with STCW Code section A-VI/1 paragraph 2 and section A-VI/6 paragraph 4, which is security awareness.

Section 15 of Marine Order 70 provides that a seafarer certificate expires on the earliest of a day determined by AMSA, the day 5 years after issue, or revocation. Revalidation requirements for ratings and the certificate of safety training are in Schedule 4 of [Marine Order 73 (Ratings) 2014](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2014L00181/latest):

items: **Option 1:** documented qualifying seagoing service of 12 months in the 5 years before applying, or 3 months in the 6 months before applying, plus maintained competence in personal survival techniques (Table A-VI/1-1), fire prevention and firefighting (Table A-VI/1-2) and security awareness (Table A-VI/6-1).
**Option 2:** without that sea service, approved courses in the same three areas, completed within the 5 years before applying for revalidation.

blocks.text: Deck officers are certified under Marine Order 71 (Masters and deck officers) 2023, which requires an approved course of basic safety training complying with STCW Code section A-VI/1 paragraph 2 as a condition of certification; engineer officers are certified under Marine Order 72 (Engineer Officers) 2014. As at November 2026, Marine Order 70 was last amended from April 1, 2026 by the Marine Orders Miscellaneous Amendment Order 2026 (No. 2).

sections.heading: How can operators map STCW basic training obligations to evidence?

blocks.text: A crewing manager answering a port state control query needs to know, for each seafarer, which STCW element is due and what document proves it. The following summary, drawn from the US and Australian texts cited above (other flag states may differ), is organized that way.

blocks.text: Operators managing multinational crews usually hold this as a [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) keyed by flag state, because the same STCW obligation produces different evidence requirements under each administration.

Yes, but not yet in force. IMO's Maritime Safety Committee instructed the Sub-Committee on Human Element, Training and Watchkeeping (HTW) in April 2022 to carry out a comprehensive review of the STCW Convention and Code. Phase 1, completed at HTW 11 in February 2025, identified more than 400 gaps, according to IMO's [comprehensive review FAQ](https://www.imo.org/en/mediacentre/hottopics/pages/comprehensive-review-of-the-stcw-convention-and-code-faq.aspx).

At [HTW 12](https://www.imo.org/en/MediaCentre/MeetingSummaries/Pages/HTW-12th-session.aspx), held from February 23 to 27, 2026, the Sub-Committee began phase 2, working on chapters II and III (deck and engine departments). IMO's timeline shows the revision of chapters IV and VI, which contains basic training, as to be determined, with MSC approval of a revised treaty in 2029 or 2030 depending on progress. Until a revised Convention is adopted and in force, the current basic training and five year refresher requirements apply. Training teams should track this using a process such as [how to update training when regulations change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each STCW Code competence table as a set of knowledge and performance points, then records which points a flag state accepts through sea service and which require shore assessment. That structure lets an operator see, for each seafarer, which elements of a five year revalidation are already evidenced and which need an approved course.

faqs.q: Is STCW basic training the same as familiarization training?
faqs.a: No. Basic training is the formal competence in survival, firefighting, first aid and personal safety set by the STCW Code tables. Familiarization is ship specific instruction given before a seafarer takes up duties aboard a particular vessel. Operators need records of both, and basic training certificates do not replace ship specific familiarization.

faqs.q: Does sea service alone keep basic training valid in the United States?
faqs.a: Not entirely. One year of sea service within the last five years is accepted for some elements, but the Coast Guard only accepts approved shore based assessments for others, including immersion suit use, jumping into water, righting a liferaft, swimming and live fire extinguishing. Most mariners therefore complete a refresher course every five years.

faqs.q: What is the minimum age for an Australian certificate of safety training?
faqs.a: Section 22 of Marine Order 70 sets a minimum age of 16 years, together with completion of an approved course complying with STCW Code section A-VI/1 paragraph 2 and section A-VI/6 paragraph 4 on security awareness.

faqs.q: Will the STCW comprehensive review change the five year refresher?
faqs.a: It is not yet known. As at November 2026, IMO has scheduled revision of chapter VI, which covers basic training, for a later stage of phase 2, with adoption of a revised Convention not expected before 2029 to 2030. Until then the existing five year requirement applies.
